sections.b: Between leaving Saul's court and Saul's death, David lives as an outlaw. He lies to the priest at Nob and feigns madness in Gath (1 Samuel 21), gathers four hundred men who are in debt, distress or bitterness (1 Samuel 22:2), rescues Keilah and is nearly betrayed by it (1 Samuel 23), and twice spares Saul's life because Saul is "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24; 1 Samuel 26). Abigail turns him from a massacre (1 Samuel 25). Despairing of escape, he serves the Philistine king Achish for sixteen months, raiding desert tribes and lying about it (1 Samuel 27), and is sent home just before the battle in which Saul dies (1 Samuel 29). At Ziklag, with his town burned and his men ready to stone him, he "made himself strong in the LORD his God" (1 Samuel 30:6), and the chapter ends with the shrewd, generous leader whom Judah will crown at Hebron.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 21:1–15; 1 Samuel 22:1–2; 1 Samuel 23:1–14; 1 Samuel 24:1–22; 1 Samuel 25:1–44; 1 Samuel 26:1–25; 1 Samuel 27:1–12; 1 Samuel 29:1–11; 1 Samuel 30:1–31

common: David's refusal to kill Saul shows that he received the kingdom from God instead of seizing it.
uncommon: Some historians, such as Baruch Halpern, think the fugitive chapters were written to answer charges that David was a Philistine mercenary with a hand in Saul's death.

claude.title: Claude's reading: the bread and the sword
claude.body: My own reading: David leaves Nob with holy bread and Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 21:6, 9), and Saul's court hears of both (1 Samuel 22:10, 13). But David never uses the sword. The story that follows is about a man kept alive by what God provides, not by the giant's weapon.

sections.b: After David flees, Saul's reign becomes a manhunt. He accuses his servants of conspiracy and has Doeg kill eighty-five priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:6–19), chases David through the wilderness of Ziph, Maon and En-gedi (1 Samuel 23–24; 26), and twice weeps and admits that David is in the right (1 Samuel 24:16–21; 26:21–25). With Samuel dead and God silent, he consults a medium at Endor and hears his doom (1 Samuel 28). The next day, hard pressed by the archers on Gilboa, he falls on his own sword; the men of Jabesh-gilead rescue his body from the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31).
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 22:6–19; 1 Samuel 23:7–28; 1 Samuel 24:1–22; 1 Samuel 26:1–25; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; 1 Samuel 31:1–13

sections.b: Robert Polzin and Robert Alter trace a chain of robes through Saul's story. Saul tears Samuel's robe and hears the kingdom torn from him (1 Samuel 15:27–28). David cuts the edge of Saul's robe, and Saul admits that David will reign (1 Samuel 24:4, 20). At Endor Saul knows Samuel by his robe and hears the kingdom given to David by name (1 Samuel 28:14, 17). Each robe scene moves the kingdom one step from Saul to David.

common: Saul is a tragic figure: chosen and gifted, but undone by fear, jealousy and disobedience.
uncommon: Some literary readers, such as David Gunn, argue that Saul was a victim of a God who rejected him for small faults, more sinned against than sinning.

sections.h: The last meeting and the death on Gilboa
sections.b: Jonathan finds David at Horesh in the wilderness of Ziph and "made David's hand strong in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). He tells David plainly that David will be king and that he himself will be second, and the two renew their covenant before the LORD. They never meet again. Jonathan dies beside his father and brothers on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2), and the men of Jabesh-gilead bury his bones with Saul's. David keeps his oath to Jonathan's house by caring for his son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9).
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 23:15–18; 1 Samuel 20:12–17; 1 Samuel 31:2; 1 Samuel 31:11–13; 2 Samuel 1:25–26; 2 Samuel 9:1–13

common: Jonathan is the Bible's great example of a friend who gives up his own claim for another's good.

sections.h: Samuel's death and his word from beyond
sections.b: "Then Samuel died. All Israel came together to mourn him" (1 Samuel 25:1). The note comes in the middle of David's flight, and it leaves Saul with no prophet. In chapter 28, the narrator repeats the notice and then brings Samuel back: at Endor the woman sees an old man rising from the earth, wrapped in a robe, and Samuel speaks his last verdict on Saul (1 Samuel 28:3–19). Whether the figure was truly Samuel has been argued for two thousand years, but his words came true the next day.

Chapters 21–31 set two kings side by side. Saul has the throne, the army and the spear, but uses them to kill priests and hunt one man (1 Samuel 22:6–19). David has no throne, but he gathers the outcasts, protects towns, asks God before he acts, refuses to take the throne by murder, and makes his first law: those who guard the baggage share the spoil equally with those who fight (1 Samuel 30:24–25). The contrast shows what kind of king God wants. Saul's words to his Benjaminites, "Is the son of Jesse going to hand out fields and vineyards to every one of you?" (1 Samuel 22:7), recall Samuel's warning that a king would take fields and vineyards (1 Samuel 8:14).

common: David's restraint toward Saul teaches that kingship is God's to give, not a prize to be seized.
uncommon: Royalists of the 1600s used David's refusal to touch "the LORD's anointed" to forbid all resistance to kings; Samuel Rutherford answered in Lex, Rex that David's armed flight was lawful resistance.

sections.b: In 1 Samuel 24 and 26, David calls Saul meshiach YHWH, "the LORD's anointed," the source of the word "Messiah." He uses it as the reason he will not kill Saul: "Who has ever stretched out his hand against the LORD's anointed and gone unpunished?" (1 Samuel 26:9). Here it means simply the king God chose and had anointed. The title later passed to David's line (Psalm 2:2; Psalm 89:20) and in Jewish and Christian hope to a coming king. David himself, already anointed (1 Samuel 16:13), refuses to act as king until God makes him one.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 24:10; 1 Samuel 26:9–11; 1 Samuel 26:16; 1 Samuel 26:23; 2 Samuel 1:14–16; Psalm 2:2

sections.b: David twice goes to Achish, king of Gath: first alone, when he must feign madness to escape (1 Samuel 21:10–15), and later with six hundred men, when he becomes Achish's vassal and is given Ziklag (1 Samuel 27). The Philistine rulers distrust him and send him home before the battle (1 Samuel 29). The Philistines then defeat Israel on Gilboa, kill Saul and his sons, hang the bodies on the wall of Beth-shan, and put Saul's armor in the temple of the Ashtaroth (1 Samuel 31). Excavations at Tell es-Safi have shown Gath to have been one of the largest cities in the land in this period.

Saul had removed "the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things" from the land (1 Samuel 28:3), as the law commanded (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11). In despair he goes to a woman at Endor "who has a ghost at her call" (1 Samuel 28:7). The Hebrew ov may have first meant a pit for calling up the dead; Hittite texts use a similar word for such a pit. The Greek translators called these people "belly-talkers," and the Mishnah describes the ba'al ov making a voice seem to come from his armpit. Chronicles names Saul's visit as one cause of his death (1 Chronicles 10:13).
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 28:3; 1 Samuel 28:7–9; Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; 1 Chronicles 10:13; Isaiah 8:19

sections.b: The narrator says "the woman saw Samuel" and "Samuel said" (1 Samuel 28:12, 15), and many readers take this at face value: God sent the real Samuel to pronounce judgment, which is why the woman screamed (so the Talmud, Justin Martyr, Origen and most modern evangelicals). Others hold that a demon took Samuel's form, since God would not honor a forbidden rite (so Tertullian, Eustathius of Antioch, Gregory of Nyssa, Luther and Calvin). Still others think the woman deceived Saul, voicing a message any shrewd observer could have guessed (so the Gaon Samuel ben Hofni and Reginald Scot). All agree that the visit was forbidden and that Saul died the next day as the voice foretold.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 28:3–25; 1 Samuel 31:1–6; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14; Isaiah 8:19; Luke 16:31

common: Most Jewish readers, and many Christians, especially today, hold that Samuel really appeared, sent by God and not by the woman's skill.
uncommon: Reginald Scot (1584) argued that the woman was a ventriloquist, using the story to attack belief in witches' powers.
For centuries after Luther and Calvin, most Protestant interpreters held that a demon impersonated Samuel.

sections.h: A prophet rising from the earth
sections.b: At Endor the woman sees "a divine being" (elohim) rising up out of the earth, an old man wrapped in a robe (1 Samuel 28:13–14). Samuel complains that he has been disturbed and tells Saul, "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me" (1 Samuel 28:19). The scene shows the common Israelite belief that the dead live on, below the earth, in some form, and that the good and the wicked share the same place. The rabbis took "with me" to mean that Saul's death atoned for him (Berakhot 12b). Abigail's phrase "the bundle of the living" (1 Samuel 25:29) later became a Jewish image of the soul's safekeeping with God.

Chapters 21–31 show God's word reaching David in several ways: through the prophet Gad, who sends him back to Judah (1 Samuel 22:5); through the ephod Abiathar carries (1 Samuel 23:2–12; 30:7–8); and through Abigail, whose speech foretells his "house that stands firm" before Nathan's oracle (1 Samuel 25:28; 2 Samuel 7:16). The rabbis counted Abigail among Israel's seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a). Saul, by contrast, receives no answer "whether through dreams, through the Urim or through the prophets" (1 Samuel 28:6) and turns to a medium.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 22:5; 1 Samuel 23:2–12; 1 Samuel 25:28–31; 1 Samuel 28:6; 1 Samuel 28:15–19; 2 Samuel 7:16

sections.b: "Saul turned to the LORD with his question, but the LORD gave him no answer, whether through dreams, through the Urim or through the prophets" (1 Samuel 28:6). The verse lists the three normal ways God was expected to speak, and Saul is cut off from all of them. Dreams are named first, as a way open even to ordinary people (Numbers 12:6; Joel 2:28). Saul repeats the list to Samuel's ghost, leaving out the Urim, perhaps because he himself had killed the priests who kept the ephod (1 Samuel 28:15; 22:18).

When Abiathar escapes the massacre at Nob, he brings the ephod to David (1 Samuel 23:6). From then on David asks God simple questions and gets clear answers: Should I attack the Philistines at Keilah? Will Saul come down? Will the men of Keilah hand me over? (1 Samuel 23:2–12). After the burning of Ziklag he asks, "Should I go after this raiding band? Will I catch up with it?" and is told yes (1 Samuel 30:7–8). Saul, who killed the priests, gets no answer "by the Urim" (1 Samuel 28:6).

After Shiloh fell, Eli's descendants served at Nob, where Ahimelech kept the Presence Bread, the ephod and Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 21:1–9). When Ahimelech helps David, Saul orders the priests killed; his own guards refuse, and Doeg the Edomite kills eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod, then destroys the town (1 Samuel 22:11–19). Abiathar alone escapes and serves David until Solomon banishes him, "fulfilling the word of the LORD" against Eli's house (1 Kings 2:26–27; 1 Samuel 2:31–33).

The Presence Bread was replaced each Sabbath and eaten only by priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). Ahimelech gives the old loaves to David and his men (1 Samuel 21:6), and the Talmud infers that it was a Sabbath and teaches that saving life overrides such laws (Menachot 95b). Jesus cites the story when his disciples are criticized for picking grain on the Sabbath (Mark 2:23–28; Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5).

Saul failed to destroy Amalek (1 Samuel 15). David raids the Amalekites from Ziklag (1 Samuel 27:8), and an Amalekite band burns Ziklag and carries off its women and children (1 Samuel 30:1–2). David pursues, strikes them from twilight to the next evening, and recovers everything (1 Samuel 30:17–19). At Endor Samuel names Saul's failure against Amalek as the reason he has lost the kingdom (1 Samuel 28:18), and an Amalekite will bring David the news of Saul's death (2 Samuel 1:1–16).

Saul's chief shepherd, Doeg the Edomite, sees David at Nob, reports it, and when Saul's guards refuse, kills the priests himself (1 Samuel 21:7; 22:9–19). Some Greek manuscripts call him a Syrian (Aramean), a difference of one letter in Hebrew. The heading of Psalm 52 ties that psalm to his report, and the rabbis made him the example of the evil tongue (Arakhin 15b).

David takes his father and mother to the king of Moab at Mizpeh and asks him to shelter them "until I find out what God will do for me" (1 Samuel 22:3–4). Many readers connect this with Ruth, David's Moabite great-grandmother (Ruth 4:17). Later David fought Moab harshly (2 Samuel 8:2), and a Jewish tradition says the Moabites killed his parents, though the Bible does not say so.

Abigail is "a woman of good sense and lovely to look at," and her husband Nabal is hard and nasty (1 Samuel 25:3). When Nabal insults David's men, she loads donkeys with bread, wine, mutton, grain, raisins and figs, rides out to meet four hundred armed men, and falls at David's feet (1 Samuel 25:18–24). Her speech takes the guilt on herself, foretells David's lasting house, and reminds him that a future king will not want innocent blood on his conscience (1 Samuel 25:24–31). David blesses God and her judgment (1 Samuel 25:32–33). After Nabal's death, she becomes David's wife (1 Samuel 25:39–42). The Talmud counts her among seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a).

common: Abigail is a model of wisdom, courage and peacemaking.
uncommon: Jon Levenson and others read the marriage politically: it brought David land and standing in Calebite country around Hebron.

claude.title: Claude's reading: Abigail and Hannah
claude.body: My own reading: Abigail near the end of 1 Samuel matches Hannah at its start. Both are wise wives of men who do not understand them, both speak of God raising the humble and bringing down the proud, and both speak of a coming king (1 Samuel 2:1–10; 25:28–31).

sections.b: Six psalm titles point to these chapters. Psalm 34 is "of David, when he disguised his good sense before Abimelech" (compare 1 Samuel 21:13, where the king is Achish). Psalm 56 is set "when the Philistines seized him in Gath." Psalm 52 is tied to Doeg's report to Saul (1 Samuel 22:9). Psalm 54 is set "when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, Is not David hiding among us?" (1 Samuel 23:19; 26:1). Psalm 57 and Psalm 142 are both "in the cave" (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3). The different name in Psalm 34 may reflect a royal title or a slip in tradition.
sections.refs: Psalm 34:0; Psalm 52:0; Psalm 54:0; Psalm 56:0; Psalm 57:0; Psalm 142:0; 1 Samuel 21:10–15; 1 Samuel 22:9; 1 Samuel 23:19; 1 Samuel 24:3

sections.b: In anguish from the archers (the Greek says he was wounded), Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him: "If you don't, these uncircumcised men will come and stab me and have their cruel fun with me" (1 Samuel 31:4). When the armor-bearer refuses, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor-bearer follows him. An Amalekite later claims that he killed Saul at his request (2 Samuel 1:6–10). The rabbis saw Saul's act as a special case, done to avoid torture and the shaming of Israel (Genesis Rabbah 34:13); Augustine and later Christian writers generally judged it a sin, though some spoke of it more gently. The text itself gives no verdict.

sections.h: The men of Jabesh repay Saul
sections.b: When the Philistines nail Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan, "every man of courage" in Jabesh-gilead marches all night, takes down the bodies of Saul and his sons, burns them, buries the bones under the tamarisk at Jabesh and fasts seven days (1 Samuel 31:11–13). Saul had begun his reign by saving them from the Ammonites (1 Samuel 11). David blesses them for their loyal love (2 Samuel 2:5).

sections.h: Nabal, Abigail and the woman of Endor
sections.b: Chapter 25 is a story of hospitality refused. David's men protected Nabal's shepherds and asked for a share of the shearing feast; Nabal answered with insult (1 Samuel 25:5–11). Abigail repairs it with a lavish gift (1 Samuel 25:18). In chapter 28 the medium at Endor, whose trade Saul had banned, kills her fattened calf and bakes bread for the king who has just heard his death sentence (1 Samuel 28:21–25). And in chapter 30 David's men feed a starving Egyptian slave before they question him (1 Samuel 30:11–12).

The chapter closes with David's wives. He marries Abigail after Nabal's death, and the Hebrew adds that he "had already taken" Ahinoam of Jezreel, while Saul had given David's first wife Michal to Palti son of Laish (1 Samuel 25:39–44). Both wives go with him to Gath and are captured and rescued at Ziklag (1 Samuel 27:3; 30:5, 18). At Hebron David has six wives (2 Samuel 3:2–5), though Deuteronomy warns that a king must not take many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). Jon Levenson and Baruch Halpern proposed that Ahinoam was Saul's wife of the same name (1 Samuel 14:50), taken as a claim to the throne. Most commentators doubt it, mainly because Saul's Ahinoam was already the mother of a grown son; the note on 1 Samuel 25:43 gives both sides.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 25:39–44; 1 Samuel 14:50; 1 Samuel 27:3; 1 Samuel 30:5; 2 Samuel 3:2–5; 2 Samuel 12:8; Deuteronomy 17:17

sections.b: After the rescue at Ziklag, some of David's men refuse to give any spoil to the two hundred who were too exhausted to go on. David answers that the spoil is what the LORD has given, and that the one who stays with the gear gets the same share as the one who fights (1 Samuel 30:22–24). "From that day onward David made it a rule and a ruling for Israel" (1 Samuel 30:25). It is an early royal law protecting the weak, and it echoes Moses' division of the Midianite spoil (Numbers 31:27).

Saul was told to destroy Amalek completely, every person and every animal (1 Samuel 15:3), and spared the best. In chapter 22 he does the same thing to Nob, the town of God's priests: man and woman, child and nursing baby, ox, donkey and sheep (1 Samuel 22:19). The narrator uses the language of holy war to show how far Saul has fallen. David's raids from Ziklag, leaving "no man or woman living" (1 Samuel 27:9, 11), are told without approval and serve to hide his lies.

In these chapters God seldom acts openly, but the narrator wants the reader to see him. "God never put him into Saul's hands" (1 Samuel 23:14). A Philistine raid calls Saul away just as he closes in on David (1 Samuel 23:27–28). A deep sleep from the LORD falls on Saul's camp (1 Samuel 26:12). Abigail's arrival keeps David from bloodshed, and he blesses God for sending her (1 Samuel 25:32–34). The Philistine rulers' distrust sends David home before the battle on Gilboa (1 Samuel 29). Nabal dies when "the LORD struck" him (1 Samuel 25:38).

The Hebrew text of Samuel is often damaged, and the Greek translation and the Dead Sea Scrolls frequently preserve a better text. For chapters 21–31, the fragments listed in DJD 17 cover about ninety verses: 4QSam-b, one of the oldest biblical manuscripts (about 250 BC), has parts of 21–23, and 4QSam-a has parts of 22 and 24–31. The most significant reported scroll reading is "to fight at Jezreel" in 28:1, where the Hebrew and Greek have "to fight Israel." In these chapters the Greek helps at several points: a skipped line in 29:10 restored from the Greek; "head of your personal guard" in 22:14 where the Hebrew reads "turns aside to your guard"; "to David" in 25:22, where the Hebrew adds "enemies" to avoid having David curse himself; "Whom did you raid?" in 27:10, with the Latin; and "to you" in 28:17, with the Latin. Elsewhere the traditional Hebrew is followed, as in 25:1, 28:16 and 30:2.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 22:14; 1 Samuel 25:22; 1 Samuel 27:10; 1 Samuel 28:1; 1 Samuel 28:17; 1 Samuel 29:10; 1 Samuel 30:2

sections.b: Jonathan and David renew their covenant before the LORD at Horesh (1 Samuel 23:18). In the cave at En-gedi, Saul asks David to swear not to cut off his descendants or wipe out his name, and David swears (1 Samuel 24:21–22). David keeps both oaths in 2 Samuel, caring for Jonathan's son Mephibosheth and sparing him when Saul's other descendants are handed to the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 9; 2 Samuel 21:7). In both cases the covenant protects the weaker family once power has changed hands.

Insulted by Nabal, David swears to leave no male of his alive by morning (1 Samuel 25:22). Abigail's intervention keeps him from carrying it out, and David blesses God for it (1 Samuel 25:32–34). The episode shows an oath in anger that is better broken than kept, and it contrasts with the solemn oaths David swears to Saul and Jonathan, which he keeps (1 Samuel 24:22).

sections.h: David in the wilderness of Judah
sections.b: As a fugitive David lives in the wilderness of Judah: the strongholds of Ziph and Maon, the steep "rocks of the wild goats" and caves at En-gedi, and the barren Jeshimon (1 Samuel 23:14–24:2; 26:1–3). The heading of Psalm 63 sets that psalm "in the wilderness of Judah," and the wilderness becomes a place of testing and of trust, as it had been for Israel.

The Philistines fasten the bodies of Saul and his sons to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10–12), a public shaming. The law of Deuteronomy forbade leaving a hanged body overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23); the men of Jabesh take them down and bury them. David later gathers the bones together with those of Saul's descendants hanged by the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:12–14).

sections.h: Loyal love for a fallen king
sections.b: The men of Jabesh-gilead risk their lives to rescue Saul's body (1 Samuel 31:11–13). David tells them, "The LORD bless you! You have done this act of loyal love for your lord, for Saul" (2 Samuel 2:5), using hesed. Their act repays Saul's rescue of Jabesh at the start of his reign (1 Samuel 11). Loyal love here is remembered kindness, kept even when the one who showed it is dead and disgraced.

Twice David has Saul at his mercy and spares him: in the cave at En-gedi, where he cuts off the edge of Saul's robe (1 Samuel 24:3–7), and in Saul's sleeping camp, where he takes the spear and water jug (1 Samuel 26:7–12). Saul answers, "You have paid me back with good, and I have paid you back with evil" (1 Samuel 24:17). Christians have read the scenes with Jesus' command to love one's enemies (Matthew 5:44) and Paul's "Pay no one back evil for evil" (Romans 12:17).

While David is an outlaw, Saul gives his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish of Gallim (1 Samuel 25:44). The notice comes right after David's marriages to Abigail and Ahinoam, so the two men trade wives in a single breath: David gains a household in Judah, and Saul cuts David out of the royal family. Michal is never asked. David will demand her back as the price of a treaty with Abner, and Palti will follow her, weeping (2 Samuel 3:13–16).

After Gilboa the Philistines cut off Saul's head and send the news to their idols (1 Samuel 31:9). Chronicles adds that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon (1 Chronicles 10:10). The scene answers an earlier one: when the ark stood in Dagon's temple at Ashdod, the god's statue fell before it with its head cut off (1 Samuel 5:4). Now it is Israel's king who loses his head in Dagon's house.
